nameStory: The "chokeberry" name comes from the astringent, mouth-puckering quality of the raw berries that makes you feel like your throat is being squeezed. The "black" part is obvious once you see the dark purple-black fruits in late summer. Despite the name, these aren't true cherries but members of the rose family!
description: Black chokeberry is a medium-sized native shrub that forms spreading clumps through underground stems. It typically grows 3-6 feet tall with glossy, dark green leaves that turn brilliant red in fall. In late spring, it produces clusters of small white or pale pink flowers, followed by dark purple-black berries in late summer that often persist into winter.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark purple-black berries about the size of large peas, growing in flat-topped clusters. The berries have a distinctive dry, puckery taste and often have tiny dried sepals (flower parts) still attached at the bottom, giving them a small crown-like appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, oval leaves with finely toothed edges that feel smooth and leathery to the touch. They're arranged alternately on the stem and have tiny dark glands along the midrib that you can see if you look closely.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale pink flowers with five petals, clustered together in flat-topped groups at the branch tips. Each flower has numerous stamens (pollen-bearing parts) that give the cluster a slightly fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading colonies through underground stems, creating patches of multiple upright stems. Individual stems are smooth and reddish-brown, and the shrub has a somewhat rounded, bushy appearance.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-brown bark on younger stems that feels slightly rough to the touch. Older stems may develop shallow furrows but remain relatively smooth compared to many other shrubs.

habitat: Black chokeberry thrives in acidic, moist soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade, making it common in wetland edges, boggy areas, and acidic woodlands. You'll often find it in the understory of pine and oak forests, along pond margins, and in areas with sandy or peaty soils throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and glossy, followed by clusters of white to pale pink flowers in May. The flowers have a subtle, sweet fragrance that attracts various pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain dark green and glossy while small green berries develop and gradually darken. By late summer, the berries ripen to their characteristic dark purple-black color.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange, and purple, making this one of our most reliable shrubs for fall color. The dark berries contrast beautifully with the colorful foliage.
seasonality.winter: Bare reddish-brown stems often retain dried berry clusters, and you can identify it by its smooth bark, colonial growth pattern, and persistent fruit remnants.

funFact: Black chokeberry has one of the highest antioxidant levels of any North American fruit—even higher than blueberries and cranberries—which has made it a superfood sensation in recent years, though indigenous peoples have known about its nutritional value for centuries!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red chokeberry, but black chokeberry has completely hairless leaf undersides (red chokeberry is fuzzy underneath) and pure black berries rather than red ones. Remember: "Black chokeberry = bald leaves underneath."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "chokeberry," this plant is completely unrelated to true cherries and is perfectly safe to eat—just very astringent when raw. The berries become much more palatable when cooked with sugar, and they're increasingly popular in jams, juices, and health foods.
compareHints: Black chokeberry differs from its close relative red chokeberry primarily in fruit color and leaf texture—black chokeberry has hairless leaves and black fruit, while red chokeberry has fuzzy leaf undersides and red to dark red berries. Both species can sometimes hybridize where they grow together, creating purple-berried intermediates.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red chokeberry is distinguished from its close relative black chokeberry by its red berries (black chokeberry has purple-black berries) and slightly taller growth habit.
